newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Thomson saga slows Europe's defence revamp.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thomson saga slows Europe's defence revamp.

text.p: The French government's decision last week to halt the sale of its 58 percent stake in defence firm Thomson-CSF dashes prospects for a major consolidation of the European defence industry this year.

But analysts and industry executives say that while the French firm might be left behind, it is just too big to be ignored in efforts to bring European firms together to match the might of U.S. rivals which have rapidly merged since the end of the cold war.

"European consolidation means the consolidation of all of the key companies within Europe...There must be a way of accommodating a market as important as the French but it is just not going to be on the timescale that is going to be possible elsewhere," said an official with one major European defence company.

The industry holds out hopes that the Thomson saga is still far from over, taking comfort from the vagaries of the French government's statement on Friday which left open the prospect of some sort of cross-border consolidation.
On Tuesday the government denied that it has made any decisions about alliances for Thomson.
"No choice has been made regarding Thomson, as far as the operator itself is concerned nor as far as alliances to be made are concerned," Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's office said.

In Friday's statement Jospin's administration said only that it had halted his predecessor's privatisation of Europe's biggest defence electronics firm and wanted to keep a "decisive state shareholding."

The government said it would propose an alternative solution and would issue new guidelines for promoting European defence cooperation but intended to use Thomson-CSF to create "a French professional and defence electronics pillar."

"We are disappointed that the (Thomson) privatisation programme appears to have been delayed...but what does a 'decisive' element mean?," said a spokesman for British Aerospace Plc, leading proponent of European consolidation and backer of Lagardere's bid for Thomson.

A blocking share would not necessarily preclude cross-border alliances, analysts say. British Aerospace itself is also still strapped by a foreign ownership limit imposed by the British government of 29.9 percent, but that did not stop it forming its Matra BAe Dynamics missiles joint venture last year with Lagardere. "There could still be ways in which partial privatisation of Thomson could follow," said Chris Avery, London-based industry analyst with Paribas Capital Markets.

But analysts say the delay will encourage Europe's leading defence groups outside France, namely British Aerospace, The General Electric Co and Daimler-Benz unit Daimler-Benz Aerospace (Dasa) to look for other deals to build up critical mass to take on U.S. combines Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman, Boeing Co with McDonnell Douglas and Raytheon with Hughes.
Dasa said this week that it believed European consolidation would proceed with or without Thomson but was awaiting clarification of French government intentions.

So far GEC, which was seen to have most to gain from combining its own defence electronics businesses with Thomson, has also adopted a wait and see attitude and declined to comment on the French government's move.

BAe and GEC have already made it known that they are looking for other deals both in Europe and in the United States, but analysts say U.S. technology export restrictions and the sheer scale of the U.S. giants means European consolidation must come first before any big transatlantic deals could be done. "Neither of them (BAe or GEC) can ever give up on Europe," said Avery. "Both of them are far too heavily involved and Thomson is too big a European business for GEC to turn its back on..."
"The sheer difference in scale means that European companies need to be bigger first in order to have a proper transatlantic merger," said one industry source.
The hold-up on the Thomson privatisation has prompted fresh media speculation that BAe and GEC will decide to merge instead.
Neither company will rule out the idea and say there could be cost savings from such a move due to some overlaps in their operations.

But analysts say such a move is now likely to be later rather than sooner since GEC has just embarked on a major restructuring aimed at moving away from its joint venture culture and instead making its wholly-owned Marconi defence arm the core business.

Managing director George Simpson announced last week that he was considering floating off the Anglo-French rail and power joint venture with Alcatel Alsthom and was also reviewing its GPT telecoms joint venture with Germany's Siemens which together accounted for 40 percent of group sales last year.
Until the joint ventures have been sorted it may be difficult to agree merger terms with BAe.

"It would be difficult," said Chris Avery. "So much of GEC's turnover is locked up in joint ventures where the exit route from the ventures is not clear and therefore the valuation would be very problematical," he said.
